title: Constructors and Destructors
learning_outcomes: Explain what constructors and destructors contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: __construct().
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Object-oriented code groups state and behavior. Classes should protect their invariants, expose a clear public API, and use inheritance only when the subtype relationship is meaningful. In this lesson, focus on __construct(); then compare it with constructor arguments. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use constructors and destructors when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Object-oriented code groups state and behavior. Classes should protect their invariants, expose a clear public API, and use inheritance only when the subtype relationship is meaningful. For constructors and destructors, begin with __construct(). Also distinguish constructor arguments; object initialization; __destruct(). Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Constructors and Destructors
content_blocks.code:
<?php
interface Describable { public function describe(): string; }
final class Product implements Describable { public function describe(): string { return "Product ready"; } }
echo (new Product())->describe() . PHP_EOL;

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
